blocks.text: Now, that the stellio is said to take hold with its hands, I refer either to its manner of moving or to its hunting. For when it walks upside down, hanging from a ceiling, it must either fix its little claws in small cracks or clasp with its hands whatever projects or is rough. That it walks upside down is stated in express words by the Philosopher, History book 9, chapter 9, where he speaks of the woodpecker thus: Πορεύεται ὕπτιος καθάπερ οἱ ἀσκαλαβῶται [poreuetai hyptios kathaper hoi askalabōtai]· It walks upside down like stellios. And in the Mirabilia: Τὸν δρυοκολάπτην τὸ ὄρνεον ἐπὶ τῶν δένδρων βαδίζειν φασὶν ὥσπερ τοὺς ἀσκαλαβώτας, καὶ ὕπτιον, καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν γαστέρα [ton dryokolaptēn to orneon epi tōn dendrōn badizein phasin hōsper tous askalabōtas, kai hyption, kai epi tēn gastera]· They say that the woodpecker walks on trees like stellios, both upside down and face down. It is surprising that Pliny renders ἀσκαλαβώτας [askalabōtas] as feles [cats], and ὕπτιον [hyption] as in subrectum [upwards] instead of supinus [upside down], when he says in book 10, chapter 18, that the tree-hollowers (that is, δρυοκολάπτας [dryokolaptas], woodpeckers) climb upwards in the manner of cats. All the more so since the same author, in book 29, chapter 4, acknowledges that the stellio is called in Greek colotes, ascalabotes and galeotes, so that no one should think Pliny was ignorant of the Greek names of the stellio. Similar is what we read in Plutarch's book On the Face in the Orb of the Moon: that what the geographers teach is highly paradoxical, ἀντίποδας οἰκεῖν, ὥσπερ θρίπας, ἢ γαλεώτας, τραπέντα ἄνω τὰ κάτω, τῇ γῇ προϊσχομένους [antipodas oikein, hōsper thripas, ē galeōtas, trapenta anō ta katō, tē gē proischomenous], that antipodes inhabit the earth, who, like woodworms or stellios, cling to the earth with the lower parts of their bodies turned upward. There too the first translators had written feles [cats] for stelliones [stellios].

We have said that the stellio also uses its hands for hunting, when it catches flies or spiders. Bustamantinus: It seizes with its hands things that promise safety. Indeed its deceptive feet, which were bound to serve for movement, take the place of hands and carry out the plunder; and those are hands to it, the feet on which it rests in moving, and those are feet, the hands with which it seizes its prey. Rightly, then, does Solomon say, The stellio takes hold with its hands, whether it walks upside down or throws itself upon its prey. Both are marvellous and most worthy of note in a tiny creature. The Greeks have here Καλαβώτης χερσὶν ἐρειδόμενος [Kalabōtēs chersin ereidomenos]; and Jerome, The stellio leans on its hands; the Arabic translator also, يتنسد بيديه [yatanassad bi-yadayhi], it leans on its hands: as if referring these words to its manner of moving. But no one could easily say what אקמתא דמסככה בידיה in the Chaldee means. For I do not [II, 519] understand what the Latin version means, The spider makes coverings with its hands. Nor much better is Gabriel, who rendered the same words of the Syriac paraphrase thus: The stellio, which creeps with its hands. I would rather read sepit [fences]; for סכך means to fence. But why the stellio should be said to fence or to make coverings, I do not understand at all. Drusius also stuck here, Observations book 10, chapter 6, and he suspects the passage of corruption. And instead of מסככה, fences or covers, he would read sometimes מסבכה, with Beth, entangling or making an intricate work, which would be said of the spider's web; sometimes מסמכה, leaning, which would be said of the stellio: so that the Chaldee would thus agree with the Greek and the Roman translators. But it is better to reconcile the Chaldee translator with the Hebrew text, in which חפש means to take hold. Accordingly Theodotion had rendered ἐλλαμβανόμενος [ellambanomenos]. I would therefore prefer to read, instead of מסככה mesacceca, מפככה mephacceca, Pe for Samech, letters not altogether unlike in shape. For פכך is in Chaldee the same as חפש in Hebrew, to catch, to take hold. Thus Prov. V, 22. in the Venice edition: With the cords of his sins אתפכך, he is caught or taken hold of.
